replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into ChatGPT, the model never actually sees that word.

It sees three pieces instead: **"un"**, **"believ"**, **"able"** — each converted to a number.

That's **tokenization** — the very first thing that happens the moment you hit send.

Every word (or word-chunk) in your prompt gets sliced into tokens, and each token gets mapped to a number. GPT-4 has a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 of these tokens. Your entire prompt becomes a list of integers before the model touches it.

Here's why this matters: "bank" is one token — but does it mean a riverbank or a financial institution? The tokenizer doesn't know yet. That ambiguity gets passed forward.

[EX]The sentence "I went to the bank to fish" and "I went to the bank to deposit money" tokenize almost identically — same numbers, different meanings. The model has to figure out which is which from context.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization turns your words into numbers — and that's the only form an LLM ever reads your prompt.[/KEY]

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually convert your words into before the model processes them?
A) A list of numbers representing word-chunks
B) A direct lookup in a memorized database
C) A search query sent to the internet
ANS: A
[/Q]

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into ChatGPT, the model doesn't see that word at all.

It sees three separate chunks: **"un"**, **"believ"**, and **"able"**.

That's because the first thing an LLM does with your prompt isn't read it — it *slices* it.

---

This slicing process is called **tokenization**.

Your text gets broken into tokens — fragments that might be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark, or even a space.

[EX]GPT-4 uses a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 tokens. The sentence "I went to the bank" becomes something like ["I", " went", " to", " the", " bank"] — five tokens. But "bank" is ambiguous: river bank or money bank? At this stage, the model doesn't know yet. It just has a number.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into a sequence of numbers — that's the only thing the model actually processes.[/KEY]

Each token gets mapped to a unique ID (just an integer), and from there it enters the model as a number, not a word.

[Q]
What is a token in an LLM?
A) A fragment of text mapped to a number — could be a word, part of a word, or punctuation
B) A single word, always
C) A copy of the original sentence stored in memory
ANS: A
[/Q]

Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "bank" into an LLM, the model has **no idea** what a bank is.

What is a token?

B) A small text chunk converted to a number for the model to process
